episodes.210106: On March 7, a cold front approaching South Texas interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass already in place across the region, leading to the development of showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. Deep Gulf moisture transported northward by a strengthening low-level jet combined with strong upper-level dynamics and steep mid-level lapse rates to create an environment supportive of organized convection. Daytime heating ahead of the front further destabilized the atmosphere, with moderate to strong instability and strong deep-layer shear promoting storm development by late afternoon.||Storms moved into the region between approximately 4 PM and 6 PM, with conditions supportive of severe thunderstorms. The primary severe hazard was large hail, particularly across the Brush Country where lapse rates were steepest and instability was greatest.
episodes.210163: A weakening cold front brought about 2 wind damage reports in Northeast South Carolina during the late afternoon hours.
episodes.210817: Thunderstorms moved through Galveston Bay and off the coast, producing strong wind gusts.
episodes.211810: A supercell thunderstorm developed just off the plateau of the Sierra Madre and moved along the Rio Grande along the Zapata/Starr Countyline before moving into and across southern Starr County between 1126 PM March 7 and 1204 AM CST March 8. This severe thunderstorm went on to produce a persistent wet microburst, which produced wind-driven large hail damage and wind damage near and around Rio Grande City and Roma. Three people were injured in their car after a gas station canopy collapsed onto their vehicle in east Rio Grande City.||A second wave of heavy rainfall moved along the Rio Grande between Roma and Rio Grande City between midnight and 2 AM, pushing already filled culverts and arroyos over their limits and produced a significant flash flood in Roma early on March 8th.
episodes.211811: There was a report of a Landspout that developed in association with a few thundershowers or streamers in Coastal Willacy County during the afternoon of March 8.
episodes.211819: A cold front associated with an upper-level system moved into the local area from the northwest on March 7th. As the upper trough weakened, the front began to stall across the region. Ample moisture was already in place across southeast Louisiana, as evidenced by the afternoon KLIX sounding, which showed record precipitable water values. In addition, sufficient instability aloft supported persistent and robust thunderstorm development. The combination of these factors resulted in widespread flash flooding across the Baton Rouge metropolitan area.
episodes.211820: A cold front associated with an upper-level system moved into the local area from the northwest on March 7th. As the upper trough weakened, the front began to stall across the region. Ample moisture was already in place across south Louisiana and south Mississippi, as evidenced by the afternoon KLIX sounding, which showed record precipitable water values. In addition, sufficient instability aloft supported persistent and robust thunderstorm development along and ahead of the boundary. The combination of these factors resulted in flash flooding across portions of southwest Mississippi.
episodes.211961: A cold front and upper disturbance moved across the region during the 8th producing pockets of heavy rain. A few reports of flooding were received.
episodes.211974: Thunderstorms developed along a slow moving cold front as it pushed south through the state. Scattered strong to severe storms also developed just ahead of this front.
episodes.212074: A cold front brought two rounds of showers and thunderstorms to South-Central Texas. As the front moved southward it produced a few storms with large hail. The next morning it moved back northward as a warm front and produced heavy rain that led to minor flooding.
episodes.212367: Strong thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of March 8, 2026 over inland Southwest Florida along the Gulf sea breeze.

An NWS Storm Survey conducted on March 8th found a track of wind damage from Roma High School to the east side of the city neighborhood grid.  Average wind speed for all damage points was estimated at 65 mph, though the surveyed swath suggested 60 to 70 mph in the area. Damage included the following:|* Temporary fencing and benches blown down, field goal posts bent, and a sign adjacent to the baseball field bent of out the ground at Roma High School.|*Large wooden pole holding an election billboard ripped out of the ground across from the school.|*Several medium to large branches of healthy mesquite trees blown down in City of Roma neighborhoods.|*Electrical pole leaning at a 30 degree angle in the City of Roma.
Street flooding occurring near the intersection East Grant Street and Thomas H. Delpit Drive.

Damaging winds, mainly to poorly built structures, combined with wind-driven hail (generally between 1 and 2.75 in diameter) caused widespread damage in the western side of Rio Grande City, from Zinnia St. near N. Alvarez Road to neighborhoods along and just south of Eisenhower Rd. in the northwest side of the City.  ||Based on the survey and surrounding reports, as well as quality of building construction, the estimated wind was 65 to 70 mph in most areas.  This included locations with wind-driven hail south of Eisenhower Rd.  Specific damage included:|*A sheet-metal roof blown off  a residence, part of which collapsed into the home and trapped a resident, who was uninjured.|*Wind-driven hail damage to at least 100 single-family residences along Santa Lucia, Santa Maria, and Santa Isabel Roads.  The vast majority of damage was shattered windows to every home surveyed.|*Direct wind damage to homes, including peeled-back shingles from 5 to more than 20% to at least a dozen structures, several fences blown down, and flipped trampolines|*A destroyed permanent food-truck canopy (blown off) which did not have appropriate rebar reinforcement, which led to collapse of the support concrete poles.  This building was fully exposed to the microburst winds, which came from the northwest.||Damage values provided are estimated, but include the combination of direct wind as well as wind-driven hail situations.

Initial reports from law enforcement and other local sources were confirmed by an NWS survey, which discovered hailstones ranging from 1 (quarter) to 2.75 (baseball) sized in and around the area surveyed for wind-driven hail damage.  Video/photo evidence provided by residence along the survey route confirmed the varied sizes of hail, which covered the ground and piled up briefly on north sides of impacted homes. ||At least one SUV, and several windows, had hail imprints that ranged from 1 to 2.75 diameter.  Note that damage value estimates from the wind-driven hail are provided in the thunderstorm wind event in this episode.

As part of a storm survey in and near Rio Grande City, damage was assessed at and near the Starr County/Rio Grande City Regional Airport.  Based on the damage, winds were estimated at 70 mph.  Damage included:|*Five large mesquite tree limbs blown down in a 100-yard diameter across the street from the airport.|*A garage door was blown in on the airport grounds, and roof panels were lifted by the wind after entering the structure.  The garage was not hurricane rated; it did not have any metal/aluminum cross-beams.

The storm survey investigated an incident at a fuel service station on the east side of Rio Grande City.  The gull canopy tipped over with bent columns at foundation. No other damage in area was noted, so wind speed at the site was estimated to be 65 to 70 mph.   The canopy collapsed onto a pickup truck underneath, and injured one adult and two children inside. Wind driven hail may have also been a factor based on vehicle impacts near the location.
